description_full: Terreno Realty Corporation an acquirer, owner and operator of industrial real estate in six major coastal U.S. markets. The firm announced today that it has executed new renewal leases totaling 233,000 square feet at Countyline Corporate Park Phase III in Hialeah, Florida. Countyline Corporate Park Buildings 26 and 28 total 422,000 square feet and are currently 100% leased to six tenants with 83,000 square feet expiring April 2027. To facilitate the new leases, Terreno Realty Corporation has executed an early termination effective July 31, 2026, with the tenant that was to expire April 2027. A provider of turbine engine disassembly, repair, logistics and storage services will relocate from 106,000 square feet in Building 28 expiring April 2030 to 83,000 square feet in Building 26. The lease will commence August 1, 2026, and expire March 2035. Terreno Realty Corporation has executed an early renewal and expansion lease with a global wholesale packaging provider in Building 28. The early renewal for 43,000 square feet will commence October 1, 2027, and expire January 2035. The expansion lease for 106,000 square feet is expected to commence November 1, 2026, and will expire in January 2035. After commencement of the new leases Countyline Corporate Park Buildings 26 and 28 will be 100% leased to five tenants. Terreno Realty Corporation acquires, owns and operates industrial real estate in six major coastal U.S. markets: New York City/Northern New Jersey; Los Angeles; Miami; San Francisco Bay Area; Seattle; and Washington, D.C. Terreno Realty Corporation was incorporated on 6th November 2009 and is based in Bellevue, United States.

financial_summary: Terreno Realty Corporation is a mid-cap real estate business with a $7.3B market cap on $476M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +20% over the past three years and +17% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

The business throws off $208M in free cash flow — roughly 44 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.67×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 7.6× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss.
Net dilution runs at 1.0% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 13% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 16% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 19% and a beta of 0.85, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.15 vs 5y 0.82), so read it loosely.
About $45.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 31% in the 2020 crash and 38% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $12.08 (margin of safety -450%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 22%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $7.87 to $18.34 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Real Estate peers: EV/EBITDA 26.1 vs 16.3 and P/FCF 35.0 vs 17.8 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.9% (below the risk-free rate).
The 17 covering analysts target $73.59 on average, 11% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 21.5% annual cash-flow growth, 23pp more than the model expects.
prof: It converts 44% of revenue into free cash flow, or 40% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only 0.67x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 44%.
ROE of 10% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 3.7% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 7.6x net debt to EBITDA ($25.0M of cash against $943.3M of debt).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 19.9% over 3 years, 20.6% over 5 years and 17.4% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 19%).
Free cash flow has compounded 24.6% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 21.9% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (13.3% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 61, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 16.8% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.9%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $1.8M sold).
Net share issuance leaves shareholder yield negative (-1.0%), diluting holders.
The share count has grown 7.9% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 14 consecutive years, raising it 22.2% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 10.2% of the float, 8.3 days to cover.
people: With about 47 employees, each generates about $10.1M of revenue, 4.4x the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 26.6% a year.
That works out to $4.4M of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $810K (0x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
